analysis.one_liner: Gives regulators, employers, and patients stronger tools to sue insurers who shortchange mental health coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee on May 13, 2022, and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law requires health plans to cover mental health and addiction treatment on equal terms with physical health care, but insurers often restrict it anyway and enforcement has been weak. This bill would let the Labor Department, employers, and patients themselves sue health plans over parity violations, would extend liability to the companies that administer and manage these benefits, and would give the Labor Department $275 million over ten years for audits, investigations, and enforcement. It died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People with employer-sponsored or individual health insurance who need mental health or substance use disorder treatment. Today, insurers must cover these conditions on par with physical illness, but enforcement relies mainly on complex private lawsuits, and claims are often denied or limited. The bill would give the Labor Department explicit power to sue plans and contractors, and would give patients and employers a clearer right to recover losses, reform discriminatory plan terms, and have denied claims re-paid.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People needing mental health or addiction treatment

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new private right of action letting patients sue their plan for mental health parity violations and recover losses.
Allows the Labor Department to sue plans and require re-adjudication (re-payment) of wrongly denied mental health claims.
Appropriates $275 million, available through 2032, for audits, investigations, enforcement, and litigation, with $240 million to the Employee Benefits Security Administration.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, employer health plans, third-party administrators, managed behavioral health organizations, and pharmacy benefit managers, which would face new lawsuits, audits, and liability for parity violations and wrongful claim denials. The $275 million appropriation would be federal spending.

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates $275 million over ten years in new enforcement funding, a real federal cost that would come from general treasury revenues rather than from the insurers or plans being regulated.

By extending liability to contractors such as pharmacy benefit managers and managed behavioral health organizations, the bill increases litigation risk for employer-sponsored benefit plans, which critics could argue raises compliance costs that are ultimately passed to plan sponsors and, indirectly, to premiums.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real: existing mental health parity rules are widely underenforced, and private lawsuits under ERISA have produced little relief, so dedicated funding and clear enforcement authority could change that for millions of people. The costs are modest and acknowledgeable: a $275 million appropriation and increased legal exposure for employer-sponsored plans, which could pass some compliance costs to premiums; broader litigation could also generate disputes over what counts as a parity violation. On balance, the public benefit of enforceable mental health coverage outweighs these costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and sat there until Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 13, 2022, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
No further action was taken: the committee never held a hearing or approved the bill, and neither the House nor the Senate ever voted on it before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

The bill would have amended ERISA so that patients, plan participants, and the Labor Secretary could sue group health plans, insurers, and contractors like pharmacy benefit managers for mental health parity violations, and would have provided $275 million in enforcement funding.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and the contractors who administer behavioral health benefits remain shielded from private enforcement of mental health parity rules, so they keep the savings from restrictive coverage; patients with mental health and substance use needs are no better off.

for.name: Rep. Joe Courtney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it.

for.name: Rep. Donald Norcross
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's one cosponsor.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor or scheduled committee action on it.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsor and cosponsor were Democrats, and the bill never advanced far enough for a roll-call vote, so no record shows how either party would have voted.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: The bill makes health plans and their contractors directly liable for parity violations, with patients and the Labor Department able to sue to recover losses and re-pay denied claims. This costs them money they currently avoid because parity rules are weakly enforced.

industries.industry: Third-party administrators, managed behavioral health organizations, and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: For the first time, companies that administer or manage behavioral health benefits could be sued if they participate in or conceal a parity violation or wrongful claim denial, closing a loophole in existing law.
